abstract.p: The poem starts with a philosophical idea: the Greeks supposedly describe a human as an inverted tree: roots in the air (the soul), branches in the earth (the body). The speaker immediately challenges that idea, saying it doesn’t quite fit, because normal trees bear fruit in autumn, at the natural end of their cycle. But this “tree” (the dead person) produces its “fruit” in spring—too early. That’s the key emotional point: a life cut short before its proper season. The “golden fruit” represents the person’s virtue or worth, and Proserpine (queen of the underworld) sees it and takes it. The comparison to the Hesperian apples (mythical golden apples) just reinforces how exceptional this “fruit” is. Out of a kind of jealous desire, she takes both the fruit and the tree—meaning the person’s promise and their life together—so nothing is left behind to fade. The ending softens that loss: although the tree is gone from this world, it “springs afresh in the Elysian field”—the classical afterlife for the virtuous.

lg.l: Greece likneth man to an inverted tree;
Whose boughs the roots, whose roots the boughs should bee.
Greece dot’s dotes in this, for trees their fruite do doth bring
In Autumne, here’s a tree brings his in spring;
A golden fruit, which when Procerpine spies,
The Hesperian appl’s match not in her eies:
Thus jealous of fruit the fruit , even both together
Takes take fruite and tree, least fruite they both do pluckt it chance to wither
And now the tree which doth spring when once this fruite did yeild
Doth spring a fresh in the Elyzian feild.

div.head: Historical context and dating
div.p: William Blagrave matriculated from Magdalen Hall, Oxford on 12 December 1600 at the age of fourteen, described as plebeii filius of Berkshire. He was admitted to St John’s College, Oxford as a Founder’s Kin Fellow in 1604, and was present in the college in 1610 to swear the oath of allegiance. He served as Dean of Law in 1613–14, and was ordained in the Church of England, being made deacon on 25 February 1616 and priest on 12 March 1620. He acted as bursar during the first part of 1620–21. Records also indicate that he was sued for debt in the Chancellor’s Court on at least four occasions between 1615 and 1621; and his death was announced in the course of legal proceedings in 1621 (Hegarty 2011).
